Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 110, verses 1–3:

It is Medinan without any disagreement.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "﴿When the help of God and the victory come﴾ was revealed in Medina."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Bazzar, Abu Yaʿla, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dalail narrated from Ibn ʿUmar that he said: "This surah was revealed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in the middle of the days of tashriq at Mina, while he was in the Farewell Pilgrimage, ﴿When the help of God and the victory come﴾, until he finished it, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) knew that it was the announcement of his farewell."

Ahmad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "When ﴿When the help of God and the victory come﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'I have been informed of the approach of my own death.'"

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him as well that he said: "When ﴿When the help of God and the victory come﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'I have been informed of the approach of my own death, and my term has drawn near.'"

al-Nasai, ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad in Zawaid al-Zuhd, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him also that he said: "When ﴿When the help of God and the victory come﴾ was revealed, the self of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was announced to him at the moment it was revealed, and he took to striving in the affairs of the Hereafter more intensely than he ever had."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Umm Habibah that she said: "When ﴿When the help of God and the victory come﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'God has not sent any prophet except that his community was given to live half the lifespan of the prophet before him. Jesus son of Mary remained forty years among the Children of Israel, and I have twenty years, and I shall die in this year.' Fatimah wept, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'You are the first of my family to join me,' and she smiled."

al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "When ﴿When the help of God and the victory come﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) called Fatimah and said: 'I have been informed of the approach of my own death.' She wept, then laughed, and said: 'He told me that his own self had been announced to him, so I wept.' He said: 'Be patient, for you are the first of my family to join me,' so I laughed." It has already been mentioned in the tafsir of Surat al-Zalzalah that this surah equals a quarter of the Qur'an.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

al-Nasr (help): assistance, derived from their saying: "The rain helped the land (naṣara al-ghayth al-arḍ)" when it aided its vegetation and prevented its drought. From this is the poet's saying:

"When the sacred month has passed, bid farewell to the lands of Tamim and give help to the land of ʿAmir."

One says: "He helped him against his enemy (naṣarahu ʿalā ʿadūwihi), yanṣuruhu, naṣran," meaning he aided him. The noun is al-nuṣrah, and "istanṣarahu ʿalā ʿadūwihi" means he asked him to help him against him.

al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: "When the help of God comes to you, O Muhammad, against those who opposed you, namely the Quraysh, and the victory," which is the conquest of Mecca. It was said that the intended meaning is his (ﷺ) help against the Quraysh without specification; it was said that it is his help against those among the disbelievers who fought him; it was said that it is the conquest of the rest of the lands; and it was said that it is what God opened for them of knowledge. He expressed the attainment of help and victory by "coming" to indicate that both are directed toward him (ﷺ).

It was said that "idhā" means "qad" (indeed), and it was said that it means "idh" (when).

al-Razi said: The difference between help (nasr) and victory (fath) is that fath is the attainment of the sought objective that had been closed, while nasr is like the cause of fath. Therefore he began with mention of nasr and followed it with fath. Or it may be said: nasr is the completion of the religion, and fath is the coming of the world, which is the completion of blessing. Or it may be said: nasr is triumph, and fath is Paradise. This is the meaning of his words.

It is said that the matter is clearer and more evident than this: nasr is the support by which the enemies are subdued and overpowered and one gains dominance over them, while fath is the conquest of the dwellings of the enemies and entering their homes.

﴿And you see the people entering the religion of God in multitudes﴾: that is, you see people from among the Arabs and others entering the religion of God with which He sent you in groups, one multitude after another.

al-Hasan said: When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) conquered Mecca, the Arabs said: "As for Muhammad having prevailed over the people of the Sacred Precinct, whom God protected from the companions of the Elephant, you have no power against him." So they entered the religion of God in multitudes, meaning many groups, after they had been entering one by one and two by two, until a whole tribe would enter Islam together.

ʿIkrimah and Muqatil said: By "the people" he meant the people of Yemen, because seven hundred men came from Yemen as believers. The accusative of "afwājan" is a circumstantial state (ḥāl) from the subject of "yadkhulūn." The position of "yadkhulūna fī dīni Allāh" is accusative as a circumstantial clause if the seeing is visual (baṣariyyah); if it is in the sense of knowledge (ʿilm), it is in the accusative position as the second object.

﴿So glorify with the praise of your Lord﴾: this is the answer of the conditional, and it is what governs it, and the sense is: "So glorify with the praise of your Lord when the help of God comes."

Makki said: The governing element of "idhā" is "jāʾa." Abu Hayyan preferred this and weakened the first view on the ground that what comes after the fāʾ of the answer does not govern what precedes it. The phrase "bi-ḥamdi Rabbika" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state; that is: "Say: Glory be to God, combined with His praise," or "praising Him."

In it is the combination of glorifying God, which indicates amazement at what He facilitated for him, something that had never occurred to his mind or the mind of anyone among the people, and praising Him for His beautiful handling of him and His great favor upon him with this blessing, which is help and victory for Umm al-Qura (the Mother of Cities), whose people had reached the utmost extremes in enmity toward him, until they expelled him from it after they had fabricated false statements and various lies, well known from their saying: "He is possessed," "He is a sorcerer," "He is a poet," "He is a soothsayer," and similar things.

Then He, glory be to Him, added to that the command to His Prophet (ﷺ) to seek forgiveness, that is: ask Him for forgiveness for your sin, humbling yourself and regarding your deeds as insufficient, and making up for what passed from you of leaving what was better. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to see his shortcoming in fulfilling God's right and would seek forgiveness and humility often, even though God had forgiven him what preceded of his sin and what followed.

It was said that seeking forgiveness by him (ﷺ) and by all the prophets is an act of worship which God imposed on them, not for asking forgiveness for a sin committed by them.

It was said that God commanded him to seek forgiveness only as an admonition to his community and an indirect address to them, so it is as if they were the ones commanded to seek forgiveness.

It was said that God commanded him to seek forgiveness for his community, not for his own sin.

It was said that by glorification here is meant prayer.

The preferable view is to take it in the sense of exalting God (tanzih), along with what we have pointed out, that it contains the sense of amazement, joy at the blessing, and happiness at what God prepared of the victory of the religion, the subduing of His enemies, the descent of humiliation upon them, and the overcoming of them.

al-Hasan said: God informed His Messenger (ﷺ) that his term had drawn near, so He commanded him to glorify and repent so that he would conclude his life with an increase in righteous deeds. He used to say often: "Glory be to You, O God, and praise be to You; forgive me, for You are the Accepting of repentance."

Qatadah and Muqatil said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) lived two years after the revelation of this surah. The clause "innahu kāna tawwāban" is a justification for his command to seek forgiveness: that is, it is among His nature to accept repentance from those who seek forgiveness from Him; He turns to them and shows mercy by accepting their repentance. "Tawwāb" is an intensive form, which indicates that He, glory be to Him, is abundant in accepting the repentance of those who repent.

al-Razi, in his tafsir, reported the consensus of the Companions that this surah indicated the announcement of the Messenger of God's (ﷺ) death.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that ʿUmar asked them about the saying of God: ﴿When the help of God and the victory come﴾. They said: "The conquest of cities and palaces." He said: "And you, O Ibn ʿAbbas, what do you say?" I said: "It is a parable struck for Muhammad (ﷺ) that his own self was announced to him."

al-Bukhari and others narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: ʿUmar used to admit me with the elders of Badr. Some of them felt something in their hearts and said: "Why does this one sit with us when we have sons like him?" ʿUmar said: "He is from whom you know." So one day he called them and admitted him among them. I did not see that he called me among them that day except to show them. He said: "What do you say about the saying of God, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿When the help of God and the victory come﴾?" Some of them said: "He commanded us to praise God and seek His forgiveness when He helps us and grants us victory." Some of them remained silent and said nothing. He said to me: "Is that what you say, O Ibn ʿAbbas?" I said: "No." He said: "What do you say?" I said: "It is the term of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), which God informed him of." He said: "﴿When the help of God and the victory come﴾ is the sign of your term ﴿So glorify with the praise of your Lord and seek His forgiveness; indeed He is ever Accepting of repentance﴾." ʿUmar said: "I know nothing of it except what you say."

Ibn al-Najjar narrated from Sahl ibn Saʿd, from Abu Bakr, that when the surah ﴿When the help of God and the victory come﴾ was revealed to the Messenger of God, it indicated that his self had been announced to him.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from ʿAʾishah that she said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to often say: 'Glory be to God and His praise; I seek His forgiveness and turn to Him in repentance.' I said: 'O Messenger of God, I see you saying often: Glory be to God and His praise; I seek forgiveness from God and turn to Him in repentance.' He said: 'My Lord informed me that I would see a sign from my community, and when I see it I should increase in saying: Glory be to God and His praise; I seek forgiveness from God and turn to Him in repentance. I have seen it: ﴿When the help of God and the victory come﴾, the conquest of Mecca, ﴿And you see the people entering the religion of God in multitudes, so glorify with the praise of your Lord and seek His forgiveness; indeed He is ever Accepting of repentance﴾.'"

al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Nasai, Ibn Majah, and others narrated from ʿAʾishah that she said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to often say in his bowing and prostration: 'Glory be to You, O God, and praise be to You; O God, forgive me.'" He was interpreting the Qur'an, meaning ﴿When the help of God and the victory come﴾. There are other hadiths on this subject.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah that he said: "When ﴿When the help of God and the victory come﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'The people of Yemen have come; they are more tender of heart. Faith is Yemeni, understanding is Yemeni, and wisdom is Yemeni.'"

al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "While the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was in Medina, he said: 'God is greatest; the help of God and the victory have come, and the people of Yemen have come, a people whose hearts are tender and whose obedience is gentle. Faith is Yemeni, understanding is Yemeni, and wisdom is Yemeni.'"

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah that he said: "I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: 'People have entered the religion of God in multitudes, and they will leave it in multitudes.'"

al-Hakim (p-1665) narrated and authenticated from Abu Hurayrah that he said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited: ﴿And you see the people entering the religion of God in multitudes﴾, and said: 'They will certainly leave it in multitudes just as they entered it in multitudes.'"

Fatimah wept, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'You are the first of my family to join me,' and she smiled."

She wept, then laughed, and said: 'He told me that his own self had been announced to him, so I wept.' He said: 'Be patient, for you are the first of my family to join me,' so I laughed." It has already been mentioned in the tafsir of Surat al-Zalzalah that this surah equals a quarter of the Qur'an.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

al-Nasr (help): assistance, derived from their saying: "The rain helped the land (naṣara al-ghayth al-arḍ)" when it aided its vegetation and prevented its drought. From this is the poet's saying:

"When the sacred month has passed, bid farewell to the lands of Tamim and give help to the land of ʿAmir."

One says: "He helped him against his enemy (naṣarahu ʿalā ʿadūwihi), yanṣuruhu, naṣran," meaning he aided him. The noun is al-nuṣrah, and "istanṣarahu ʿalā ʿadūwihi" means he asked him to help him against him.

al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: "When the help of God comes to you, O Muhammad, against those who opposed you, namely the Quraysh, and the victory," which is the conquest of Mecca. It was said that the intended meaning is his (ﷺ) help against the Quraysh without specification; it was said that it is his help against those among the disbelievers who fought him; it was said that it is the conquest of the rest of the lands; and it was said that it is what God opened for them of knowledge. He expressed the attainment of help and victory by "coming" to indicate that both are directed toward him (ﷺ).

It was said that "idhā" means "qad" (indeed), and it was said that it means "idh" (when).

al-Razi said: The difference between help (nasr) and victory (fath) is that fath is the attainment of the sought objective that had been closed, while nasr is like the cause of fath. Therefore he began with mention of nasr and followed it with fath. Or it may be said: nasr is the completion of the religion, and fath is the coming of the world, which is the completion of blessing. Or it may be said: nasr is triumph, and fath is Paradise. This is the meaning of his words.

It is said that the matter is clearer and more evident than this: nasr is the support by which the enemies are subdued and overpowered and one gains dominance over them, while fath is the conquest of the dwellings of the enemies and entering their homes.

﴿And you see the people entering the religion of God in multitudes﴾: that is, you see people from among the Arabs and others entering the religion of God with which He sent you in groups, one multitude after another.

al-Hasan said: When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) conquered Mecca, the Arabs said: "As for Muhammad having prevailed over the people of the Sacred Precinct, whom God protected from the companions of the Elephant, you have no power against him." So they entered the religion of God in multitudes, meaning many groups, after they had been entering one by one and two by two, until a whole tribe would enter Islam together.

ʿIkrimah and Muqatil said: By "the people" he meant the people of Yemen, because seven hundred men came from Yemen as believers. The accusative of "afwājan" is a circumstantial state (ḥāl) from the subject of "yadkhulūn." The position of "yadkhulūna fī dīni Allāh" is accusative as a circumstantial clause if the seeing is visual (baṣariyyah); if it is in the sense of knowledge (ʿilm), it is in the accusative position as the second object.

﴿So glorify with the praise of your Lord﴾: this is the answer of the conditional, and it is what governs it, and the sense is: "So glorify with the praise of your Lord when the help of God comes."

Makki said: The governing element of "idhā" is "jāʾa." Abu Hayyan preferred this and weakened the first view on the ground that what comes after the fāʾ of the answer does not govern what precedes it. The phrase "bi-ḥamdi Rabbika" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state; that is: "Say: Glory be to God, combined with His praise," or "praising Him."

In it is the combination of glorifying God, which indicates amazement at what He facilitated for him, something that had never occurred to his mind or the mind of anyone among the people, and praising Him for His beautiful handling of him and His great favor upon him with this blessing, which is help and victory for Umm al-Qura (the Mother of Cities), whose people had reached the utmost extremes in enmity toward him, until they expelled him from it after they had fabricated false statements and various lies, well known from their saying: "He is possessed," "He is a sorcerer," "He is a poet," "He is a soothsayer," and similar things.

Then He, glory be to Him, added to that the command to His Prophet (ﷺ) to seek forgiveness, that is: ask Him for forgiveness for your sin, humbling yourself and regarding your deeds as insufficient, and making up for what passed from you of leaving what was better. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to see his shortcoming in fulfilling God's right and would seek forgiveness and humility often, even though God had forgiven him what preceded of his sin and what followed.

It was said that seeking forgiveness by him (ﷺ) and by all the prophets is an act of worship which God imposed on them, not for asking forgiveness for a sin committed by them.

It was said that God commanded him to seek forgiveness only as an admonition to his community and an indirect address to them, so it is as if they were the ones commanded to seek forgiveness.

It was said that God commanded him to seek forgiveness for his community, not for his own sin.

It was said that by glorification here is meant prayer.

The preferable view is to take it in the sense of exalting God (tanzih), along with what we have pointed out, that it contains the sense of amazement, joy at the blessing, and happiness at what God prepared of the victory of the religion, the subduing of His enemies, the descent of humiliation upon them, and the overcoming of them.

al-Hasan said: God informed His Messenger (ﷺ) that his term had drawn near, so He commanded him to glorify and repent so that he would conclude his life with an increase in righteous deeds. He used to say often: "Glory be to You, O God, and praise be to You; forgive me, for You are the Accepting of repentance."

Qatadah and Muqatil said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) lived two years after the revelation of this surah. The clause "innahu kāna tawwāban" is a justification for his command to seek forgiveness: that is, it is among His nature to accept repentance from those who seek forgiveness from Him; He turns to them and shows mercy by accepting their repentance. "Tawwāb" is an intensive form, which indicates that He, glory be to Him, is abundant in accepting the repentance of those who repent.

al-Razi, in his tafsir, reported the consensus of the Companions that this surah indicated the announcement of the Messenger of God's (ﷺ) death.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that ʿUmar asked them about the saying of God: ﴿When the help of God and the victory come﴾. They said: "The conquest of cities and palaces." He said: "And you, O Ibn ʿAbbas, what do you say?" I said: "It is a parable struck for Muhammad (ﷺ) that his own self was announced to him."

al-Bukhari and others narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: ʿUmar used to admit me with the elders of Badr. Some of them felt something in their hearts and said: "Why does this one sit with us when we have sons like him?" ʿUmar said: "He is from whom you know." So one day he called them and admitted him among them. I did not see that he called me among them that day except to show them. He said: "What do you say about the saying of God, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿When the help of God and the victory come﴾?" Some of them said: "He commanded us to praise God and seek His forgiveness when He helps us and grants us victory." Some of them remained silent and said nothing. He said to me: "Is that what you say, O Ibn ʿAbbas?" I said: "No." He said: "What do you say?" I said: "It is the term of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), which God informed him of." He said: "﴿When the help of God and the victory come﴾ is the sign of your term ﴿So glorify with the praise of your Lord and seek His forgiveness; indeed He is ever Accepting of repentance﴾." ʿUmar said: "I know nothing of it except what you say."

Ibn al-Najjar narrated from Sahl ibn Saʿd, from Abu Bakr, that when the surah ﴿When the help of God and the victory come﴾ was revealed to the Messenger of God, it indicated that his self had been announced to him.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from ʿAʾishah that she said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to often say: 'Glory be to God and His praise; I seek His forgiveness and turn to Him in repentance.' I said: 'O Messenger of God, I see you saying often: Glory be to God and His praise; I seek forgiveness from God and turn to Him in repentance.' He said: 'My Lord informed me that I would see a sign from my community, and when I see it I should increase in saying: Glory be to God and His praise; I seek forgiveness from God and turn to Him in repentance. I have seen it: ﴿When the help of God and the victory come﴾, the conquest of Mecca, ﴿And you see the people entering the religion of God in multitudes, so glorify with the praise of your Lord and seek His forgiveness; indeed He is ever Accepting of repentance﴾.'"

al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Nasai, Ibn Majah, and others narrated from ʿAʾishah that she said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to often say in his bowing and prostration: 'Glory be to You, O God, and praise be to You; O God, forgive me.'" He was interpreting the Qur'an, meaning ﴿When the help of God and the victory come﴾. There are other hadiths on this subject.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah that he said: "When ﴿When the help of God and the victory come﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'The people of Yemen have come; they are more tender of heart. Faith is Yemeni, understanding is Yemeni, and wisdom is Yemeni.'"

al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "While the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was in Medina, he said: 'God is greatest; the help of God and the victory have come, and the people of Yemen have come, a people whose hearts are tender and whose obedience is gentle. Faith is Yemeni, understanding is Yemeni, and wisdom is Yemeni.'"

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah that he said: "I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: 'People have entered the religion of God in multitudes, and they will leave it in multitudes.'"

al-Hakim (p-1665) narrated and authenticated from Abu Hurayrah that he said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited: ﴿And you see the people entering the religion of God in multitudes﴾, and said: 'They will certainly leave it in multitudes just as they entered it in multitudes.'"
